{{Short description|Generalization of the pumping lemma for context-free languages}}
In the theory of [[formal language]]s, '''Ogden's lemma''' (named after William F. Ogden)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ogden |first=William |date=September 1968 |title=A helpful result for proving inherent ambiguity |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01694004 |journal=Mathematical Systems Theory |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=191–194 |doi=10.1007/bf01694004 |s2cid=13197551 |issn=0025-5661|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is a generalization of the [[pumping lemma for context-free languages]].

Despite Ogden's lemma being a strengthening of the pumping lemma, it is insufficient to fully characterize the class of context-free languages.<ref>{{cite conference |first=Marcus |last=Kracht |title=Too Many Languages Satisfy Ogden's Lemma |conference=Proceedings of the 27th Pennsylvania Linguistics Colloquium |pages=115–121 |date=2004 |location=Philadelphia |url=http://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/mkracht/html/ogden.pdf |access-date=16 May 2024}}</ref> This is in contrast to the [[Myhill–Nerode theorem]], which unlike the [[pumping lemma for regular languages]] is a necessary and sufficient condition for regularity.

== Statement ==

{{Math theorem
| name = Ogden's lemma
| note = 
| math_statement = If a language <math>L</math> is generated by a [[context-free grammar]], then there exists some <math>p\geq 1</math> such that for every <math>w \in L</math> with <math>|w| \geq p</math>, and for any marking of <math>p</math> or more positions in <math>w</math>, there exists a nonterminal <math>A</math> of the grammar and a way to split <math>w</math> into 5 segments <math>uxzyv</math>, such that

<math display="block">S \Rightarrow^* uAv \Rightarrow^* uxAyv \Rightarrow^* uxzyv</math>

<math>z</math> contains at least one marked position.

<math>xzy</math> contains at most <math>p</math> marked positions.

<math>u, x</math> both contain marked positions, or <math>y, v</math> both contain marked positions.
}}We will use underlines to indicate "marked" positions.

=== Special cases ===
Ogden's lemma is often stated in the following form, which can be obtained by "forgetting about" the grammar, and concentrating on the language itself:
If a language {{mvar|L}} is context-free, then there exists some number <math>p\geq 1</math> (where {{mvar|p}} may or may not be a pumping length) such that for any string {{mvar|s}} of length at least {{mvar|p}} in {{mvar|L}} and every way of "marking" {{mvar|p}} or more of the positions in {{mvar|s}}, {{mvar|s}} can be written as
:<math>s = uvwxy</math>
with strings {{mvar|u, v, w, x,}} and {{mvar|y}}, such that

#{{mvar|vx}} has at least one marked position,
#{{mvar|vwx}} has at most {{mvar|p}} marked positions, and
#<math>uv^n wx^n y \in L</math> for all <math>n \geq 0</math>.

In the special case where every position is marked, Ogden's lemma is equivalent to the pumping lemma for context-free languages. Ogden's lemma can be used to show that certain languages are not context-free in cases where the pumping lemma is not sufficient. An example is the language <math>\{a^i b^j c^k d^l : i = 0 \text{ or } j = k = l\}</math>.

== Example applications ==

=== Non-context-freeness ===
The special case of Ogden's lemma is often sufficient to prove some languages are not context-free. For example, <math>\{ a^m b^n c^m d^n | m, n \geq 1\} </math> is a standard example of non-context-free language,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hopcroft |first=John E. |title=Introduction to automata theory, languages, and computation |date=1979 |publisher=Addison-Wesley |others=Jeffrey D. Ullman |isbn=0-201-02988-X |location=Reading, Mass. |oclc=4549363|page=128}}</ref>

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

Suppose the language is generated by a context-free grammar, then let <math>p</math> be the length required in Ogden's lemma, then consider the word <math>a^p\underline{b^pc^p}d^p</math> in the language. Then the three conditions implied by Ogden's lemma cannot all be satisfied. 
}}

Similarly, one can prove the "copy twice" language <math>L=\{w^2 | w \in \{a, b\}^*\}</math> is not context-free, by using Ogden's lemma on <math>a^{2p}\underline{b^{2p}}a^{2p}b^{2p}</math>.

And the given example last section <math>\{a^i b^j c^k d^l : i = 0 \text{ or } j = k = l\}</math> is not context-free by using Ogden's lemma on <math>ab^{2p} \underline{c^{2p}}d^{2p}</math>.

=== Inherent ambiguity ===
Ogden's lemma can be used to prove the [[Ambiguous grammar#Inherently ambiguous languages|inherent ambiguity]] of some languages, which is implied by the title of Ogden's paper.

'''Example''': Let <math>L_0 =  \{a^nb^mc^m | m, n \geq 1\}, L_1 = \{a^mb^mc^n | m, n \geq 1\}</math>. The language <math>L = L_0 \cup L_1</math> is inherently ambiguous. (Example from page 3 of Ogden's paper.)

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

Let <math>p</math> be the pumping length needed for Ogden's lemma, and apply it to the sentence <math>a^{p!+p}\underline{b^pc^p}</math>.

By routine checking of the conditions of Ogden's lemma, we find that the derivation is

<math display="block">S \Rightarrow^* uAv \Rightarrow^* uxAyv \Rightarrow^* uxzyv</math>
where <math>u = a^{p! + p}b^{p - s - k}, x = b^{k}, z = b^{s}c^{s'}, y = c^k, v = c^{p - s' - k}</math>, satisfying <math>s+s' \geq 1</math> and <math>k \geq 1</math> and <math>p \geq s+s' + 2k</math>.

Thus, we obtain a derivation of <math>a^{p!+p}b^{p!+p}c^{p!+p}</math> by interpolating the derivation with <math>p!/k</math> copies of <math>A \Rightarrow^* xAy</math>. According to this derivation, an entire sub-sentence <math>x^{p!/k+1}zy^{p!/k+1} = b^{p!+k+s}c^{p!+k+s'}</math> is the descendent of one node <math>A</math> in the derivation tree.

Symmetrically, we can obtain another derivation of  <math>a^{p!+p}b^{p!+p}c^{p!+p}</math>, according to which there is an entire sub-sentence <math>a^{p!+k''+s''}b^{p!+k''+s'''}</math> being the descendent of one node in the derivation tree.

Since <math>(p!+k+s) + (p!+k''+s''') > 2p! +1 > p! + p</math>, the two sub-sentences have nonempty intersection, and since neither contains the other, the two derivation trees are different.  
}}

Similarly, <math>L^*</math> is inherently ambiguous, and for any CFG of the language, letting <math>p</math> be the constant for Ogden's lemma, we find that <math>(a^{p!+p}b^{p!+p}c^{p!+p})^n</math> has at least <math>2^n</math> different parses. Thus <math>L^*</math> has an unbounded degree of inherent ambiguity.

=== Undecidability ===
The proof can be extended to show that deciding whether a CFG is inherently ambiguous is undecidable, by reduction to the [[Post's correspondence problem|Post correspondence problem]]. It can also show that deciding whether a CFG has an unbounded degree of inherent ambiguity is undecidable. (page 4 of Ogden's paper)

{{Math proof|title=Construction|proof=

Given any Post correspondence problem over binary strings, we reduce it to a decision problem over a CFG.

Given any two lists of binary strings <math>\xi_1, ..., \xi_n</math> and <math>\eta_1, ..., \eta_n</math>, rewrite the binary alphabet to <math>\{d, e\}</math>.

Let <math>L\left(\xi_1, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right)</math> be the language over alphabet <math>\{d,e,f\}</math>, generated by the CFG with rules <math>S \to \xi_iS d^i e| f</math> for every <math>i = 1, ..., n</math>. Similarly define <math>L\left(\eta_1, \cdots, \eta_{n}\right)</math>.

Now, by the same argument as above, the language <math>(L_0 \cdot L\left(\xi_1, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right))\cup (L_1 \cdot L\left(\eta_1, \cdots, \eta_{n}\right))</math> is inherently ambiguous iff the Post correspondence problem has a solution.

And the language <math>((L_0 \cdot L\left(\xi_1, \cdots, \xi_{n}\right))\cup (L_1 \cdot L\left(\eta_1, \cdots, \eta_{n}\right)))^*</math> has an unbounded degree of inherent ambiguity iff the Post correspondence problem has a solution.  
}}

== Generalized condition ==

Bader and Moura have generalized the lemma<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bader |first1=Christopher |last2=Moura |first2=Arnaldo |title=A Generalization of Ogden's Lemma |journal=  Journal of the ACM|date=April 1982|volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=404–407 |doi=10.1145/322307.322315 |s2cid=33988796 |doi-access=free }}</ref> to allow marking some positions that are ''not'' to be included in {{mvar|vx}}. Their dependence of the parameters was later improved by Dömösi and Kudlek.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Dömösi |first1=Pál |chapter=Strong iteration lemmata for regular, linear, context-free, and linear indexed languages |date=1999 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48321-7_18 |title=Fundamentals of Computation Theory |pages=226–233 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-66412-3 |access-date=2023-02-26 |last2=Kudlek |first2=Manfred|doi=10.1007/3-540-48321-7_18 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> If we denote the number of such ''excluded'' positions by {{mvar|e}}, then the number {{mvar|d}} of ''marked'' positions must satisfy <math>d\geq p^{(e+1)}</math>, where {{mvar|p}} is some constant that depends only on the language. The statement becomes that every {{mvar|s}} can be written as
:<math>s = uvwxy</math>
with strings {{mvar|u, v, w, x,}} and {{mvar|y}}, such that

#{{mvar|vx}} has at least one marked position and no excluded position,
#Let <math>r</math> be the number of marked positions and <math>s</math> the number of excluded positions in {{mvar|vwx}}; then <math>r \leq p^{s+1}</math>.
#<math>uv^n wx^n y \in L</math> for all <math>n \geq 0</math>.
